doc_description: Developing Basketball Intelligence by Brian McCormick - tactical skills, game awareness, decision-making, drills and games.

structure.title: Developing Basketball Intelligence
structure.summary: This text is an excerpt from Brian McCormick's book 'Developing Basketball Intelligence,' aimed at advanced players and focusing on tactical skills and game awareness. It includes copyright and publication details, a list of the author's other works, and a Table of Contents covering various aspects of basketball development from individual skills to team play. The introduction defines basketball intelligence as a trainable skill encompassing tactical understanding, game awareness, and effective decision-making, characterizing intelligent players as expert performers who can read, anticipate, and execute plays effectively.

nodes.title: Characteristics of an Intelligent Player
nodes.summary: The text introduces basketball intelligence as a trainable skill that combines tactical understanding, game awareness, and decision-making. It outlines the characteristics of an intelligent player, emphasizing their ability to read, anticipate, and execute plays effectively. The "Sports Cognition Framework" is presented, highlighting decision-making ability, motor skill competence, and positive mental state as key to sports success, with a primary focus on developing decision-making skills in basketball. The text underscores the importance of quick and accurate decisions in the fast-paced game, noting that superior anticipatory performance and faster decision-making provide a significant advantage.

nodes.title: Developing Basketball Intelligence: A Tactical and Global Approach
nodes.summary: This text introduces basketball intelligence as a trainable skill that combines tactical understanding, game awareness, and decision-making. It outlines the characteristics of an intelligent player, emphasizing their ability to read, anticipate, and execute effectively. The "Sports Cognition Framework" is presented, highlighting decision-making as a key element for sports success. The text critiques the traditional belief that basketball intelligence is innate, arguing that it can be developed through improved perceptual skills and a shift from technical to tactical approaches. It advocates for a global coaching methodology and the Teaching Games for Understanding (TGfU) model, which emphasizes playing the game and problem-solving over isolated skill drills. The text also discusses the importance of attention and information processing in developing basketball intelligence, contrasting it with traditional coaching methods that prioritize immediate results over long-term player development.

nodes.title: Developing Basketball Intelligence: Perception, Attention, and Practice Methods
nodes.summary: The text explains that basketball intelligence is not a mystical ability but a result of developed perceptual and cognitive skills, including effective search strategies and pattern recognition. It highlights the importance of attention, specifically broad-external attention, in processing environmental cues and anticipating plays. The document contrasts 'open skill' sports like basketball with 'closed skill' practice, arguing that game-like situations and modified games are more effective for developing decision-making and perceptual skills. It critiques traditional block training for its short-term memory retention and advocates for random or variable practice, which promotes long-term learning. The text also discusses the role of lead cues in prompting correct responses and emphasizes deliberate practice in small-sided games as an optimal learning environment, with coaches using feedback and questions to guide player development.

nodes.title: Coaching Strategies for Developing Basketball Intelligence and Game Application
nodes.summary: This text discusses effective coaching strategies for developing basketball intelligence, emphasizing the interplay between random and block training. It highlights the use of coach-created cues, both reactive ('Base!') and proactive ('lead cues' like 'space, space'), to guide player responses and improve recognition. Deliberate practice, characterized by timely feedback, specific goals, and ample repetitions, is crucial for meaningful improvement. Small-sided games are presented as an ideal learning environment, offering a balance of repetition and game-like variables. The text advocates for coaches to stimulate player thinking through questions rather than solely providing instructions, fostering active learning and ownership. It stresses the importance of skill transfer from practice to competition by developing skills in context and emphasizing perception and decision-making. Finally, the text transitions to individual ball skills, focusing on game-like dribbling in full-court situations, where reading the defender and situational cues are paramount for success, rather than just technical execution.

nodes.title: FULL COURT SITUATIONS
nodes.summary: This section focuses on teaching players how to attack individual defenders in various game situations, emphasizing game ball handling over pure technique. It highlights that success comes from reading the defender and understanding one's strengths, rather than just technical execution. The text suggests that situational awareness, like recognizing when a hesitation move is effective, is crucial, and recommends using live games for practice against defenders.

nodes.title: Attacking a Defensive Player in Open Space
nodes.summary: The text describes strategies for an offensive player attacking a defender in open space, emphasizing the offensive player's speed advantage. It details how to read a defender's stance (parallel or top foot) and positioning (playing the ball or shoulder) to choose the most effective attack. Specific moves like speed dribbles, in-n-out, and crossovers are recommended based on these reads. The importance of straight-line drives is highlighted. The document also introduces the Foster's 1v1 Drill to practice these skills, outlining its objectives, execution, and teaching points. Finally, it addresses common player struggles, such as technical skill deficiencies or making incorrect decisions, and offers solutions like breaking down skills or simplifying defensive reads.

nodes.title: Attacking when Tightly Defended
nodes.summary: The text describes strategies for attacking a tightly defended player in a full court setting, covering two main scenarios: receiving a pass while defended and being closely guarded after dribbling. It emphasizes reading the defender's cues, such as their lead shoulder and location, to identify a path of least resistance. The offensive player's goals can range from advancing the ball to creating transition opportunities. The text outlines key questions an offensive player should ask themselves after initiating a dribble to make informed decisions. It then introduces a 'Full Court 1v1' game as a practice method, detailing its objective, prerequisites, execution, progressions, and teaching points. Finally, it advises on assessing mistakes made during the game to guide further practice, suggesting either more technical drills or increased game experience.

nodes.title: LIVE BALL SITUATIONS (HALF COURT)
nodes.summary: The text emphasizes the importance of live ball moves and 1v1 scenarios in basketball, highlighting that individual battles are crucial for team success. It argues that individual plays are increasingly vital, especially at higher levels, as they are necessary to disorganize set defenses and create offensive advantages. Players are most open when receiving passes and should capitalize on this by making individual moves against disorganized defenses or poor closeouts. A 1v1 progression is presented as a method to practice these moves and the decision-making involved.

nodes.title: Catching in Open Space
nodes.summary: This text describes strategies for 'Catching in Open Space' in basketball, focusing on how to react when receiving a pass while being defended. It emphasizes anticipating the pass, reading the defender's position and movements, and understanding various offensive options like shooting, passing to the post, or driving. The text details how to analyze a defender's closeout to determine the best course of action, whether it's a shot, a drive, a cut, or relocating. It also highlights the importance of exploiting defender's weaknesses and maintaining awareness of the overall game situation.

nodes.title: Drill: 1v1 Closeout
nodes.summary: This text describes the '1v1 Closeout' basketball drill. The objective is for the offensive player to read the defender's closeout and attack with a shot or move, utilizing the defender's momentum. Prerequisites include catch-and-shoot, lay-ups, and shot fakes. The drill involves a passer (P3), an offensive player (P1), and a defender (P2), with play continuing until a score, rebound, steal, or out of bounds. The winner stays on offense. Variations include changing starting positions, closeout angles, and dribble limits. Key teaching points emphasize knowing strengths, making decisions early, adjusting to passes, reading closeout angles, attacking momentum, and following shots.

nodes.title: Catching when Tightly Defended
nodes.summary: The text provides strategies for offensive players receiving passes while tightly defended, advising against immediate shots and instead focusing on reading the defender's momentum and positioning to make effective moves. It outlines key questions to assess the defender and emphasizes attacking their weaknesses. Two drills, '1v1 Check' and '1v1 Wing Entry', are detailed to help players assess defenses and exploit openings, with specific prerequisites, execution steps, variations, and teaching points. The text also explains fundamental offensive moves like direct and crossover drives, pivots, and the sweep and go, and how to combine them. Finally, it addresses passing, critiquing traditional instruction that overemphasizes technique and neglects the defensive aspect, introducing the concept of 'tunnel vision' and stressing the need for players to develop ball strength and a broad focus to make effective passes in game situations.

nodes.title: Defender
nodes.summary:
## Defender

- How is my defender defending me?
- Is he quick?
- Where are his hands?
- Where are his eyes?
- Does he go for fakes?
- Do I have a dribble to use to create a passing lane?

nodes.title: Target
nodes.summary:
## Target

- Is he open?
- Is he standing still or on the move?
- Does he cut aggressively to the ball?
- Is he using a screen?
- Where is he cutting?
- Is he going to curl or flare?
- Where are his eyes?
- Does he feel his defender?
- Will he respond to me if I make a pass fake to get him to cut elsewhere (fake a pass to the wing to create a backdoor cut)?
- Will he finish his cut or will he break off the cut if the pass is not immediate?
- Is he cutting to get open or is it a cut to set up a cut (v-cut)?
- Are his hands up?

nodes.title: Target's Defender
nodes.summary: The text discusses the critical considerations for a basketball player when facing a defender, including the defender's position and actions, and the target's defender's role. It emphasizes that strong ball-handling confidence allows players to focus externally on the game, enabling subconscious decision-making similar to experienced drivers. Conversely, a lack of confidence narrows a player's focus, leading to rushed decisions and errors. To combat this, the text introduces five key skills: 'The Box' for ball protection during movement, 'Space Step' for creating space, 'Diamond the Ball' for secure ball handling and readiness for various actions, 'Pass Fake' to deceive defenders, and 'Ball Fake' to create passing opportunities. These skills, along with existing ball-handling abilities, are crucial for players facing pressure defense.

nodes.title: GETTING OPEN
nodes.summary: The text focuses on the fundamental basketball skill of 'getting open' for passes, emphasizing its 1v1 nature and the importance of evasion techniques before introducing specific cuts. It outlines a training progression from general agility to structured drills and games, detailing three specific games (Volleyball Passing, Full Court 3v3/No Dribble, 2v2 Gael Passing) with their objectives, execution, and teaching points. The text also includes a variation of the 2v2 Gael Passing game and provides guidance on using games for player evaluation and identifying areas for improvement. It introduces the 1v1 Hard2Guard Drill for ball protection and discusses the importance of receiver technique, particularly running to the catch, and mentions drills for receiving under pressure.

nodes.title: Drill: 2-man Pressure Passing
nodes.summary: The 2-man Pressure Passing Drill aims to develop players' strength on the ball and their ability to make aggressive cuts. It requires several prerequisite skills like V-cuts, L-cuts, and various passes. The drill involves two lines of players where one passes to a cutting teammate, who then receives the ball with a quick stop and pivot. The drill progresses by adding defenders, emphasizing physical play, protecting the ball, and creating passing lanes. It specifically addresses common offensive mistakes such as 'dancing' with defenders, avoiding contact, and taking poor angles, by encouraging direct cuts and assertive play.

nodes.title: Drill: Box Passing
nodes.summary: This document describes the 'Box Passing' drill, designed to improve players' ability to get open and pass under pressure. It outlines the drill's objective, required pre-requisite skills (various passes and pivot foot), and detailed execution steps involving offensive and defensive players in a box formation. The drill emphasizes completing a set number of passes consecutively without turnovers, with team roles switching upon a turnover. Key teaching points include readiness to pass, defensive angle denial, using screens, physicality, and ball security.

nodes.title: Drill: The Gauntlet
nodes.summary: The text describes 'The Gauntlet' drill, designed to improve court vision and passing lane creation for advancing the ball down court. It outlines the drill's objective, prerequisites (including V-cuts, L-cuts, and fakes), execution (dividing the court into zones with defenders and offensive players attempting to score), and key teaching points (emphasizing passing over dribbling, using fakes, and following shots). It also suggests related drills for specific skill development. The second part of the text, 'Chapter 4: Transition Basketball,' highlights the significance of transition play in youth basketball, covering both offensive fast breaks and defensive full-court presses. It explains how transition situations, often arising from presses, create advantages for either offense or defense. The chapter emphasizes that small-sided games and transition plays build offensive confidence and prepare players for various game scenarios, including 'broken plays.' Ultimately, successful transition basketball relies on players' ability to read the game, make sound decisions, and execute with technical skill, guided by coaching principles.

nodes.title: 2v1 FAST BREAK
nodes.summary: The text discusses the 2v1 fast break in basketball, emphasizing the need for variable training due to the unpredictable nature of the game. It outlines three scenarios that can lead to a 2v1 break and provides general guidelines for executing it, including court spacing, aggressive attacking, and making the defender commit. Specific advice is given for the trailing offensive player and key questions players should consider. The text highlights that a successful 2v1 break should result in a lay-up and identifies common mistakes that hinder its effectiveness.

nodes.title: Games
nodes.summary: The text outlines three games (1v2/2v1, Rabbit, and 2v2 Rugby) used to develop 2v1 fast breaks and ball handling against traps. It highlights the suitability of 2v2 Rugby for young players needing space for technical skill development and for advanced players needing practice in tight spaces. The games serve to introduce transition plays and assess player execution. A detailed breakdown of the 1v2/2v1 game is provided, including its objective, required skills, drill execution, and key teaching points for offensive players.

nodes.title: Game: Rabbit
nodes.summary: The text describes a basketball drill called 'Rabbit' designed to improve open court ball handling and aggressive rebounding. It outlines the game's objective, necessary pre-requisite skills, detailed execution steps involving two teams, offensive and defensive transitions, and live play scenarios. Key teaching points emphasize floor spacing, offensive movement, quick scoring, and aggressive rebounding. The game is played to nine baskets.

nodes.title: Game: 2v2 Rugby
nodes.summary: This text describes the '2v2 Rugby' game, focusing on handling backcourt traps, creating transition baskets, and finishing lay-ups under pressure. It lists necessary prerequisite skills and details the drill execution, including team formation, scoring rules, backcourt restrictions, and sideline trapping. Key teaching points for both defense (trapping strategies) and offense (court vision, dribbling, attacking the basket) are also provided.

nodes.title: Practice
nodes.summary: This text outlines a practice methodology for identifying and correcting player errors in small-sided games. It categorizes errors into positioning, decision-making, and technical mistakes, providing specific strategies for each. Positioning issues are addressed with tactical reviews, while decision-making problems are tackled using questioning to foster player analysis and self-correction. Technical errors require focused instruction and progressive drills, with a sample lay-up drill progression provided. The text also lists common issues in 1v2, 2v1, and 2v2 scenarios and details two specific drills, the 2v1 Penetrate & Finish Drill and the 2v2 Army Drill, designed to improve player decision-making and execution in these situations, including their objectives, prerequisites, execution steps, and key teaching points.

nodes.title: Drill: 2x2 Foster's Drill
nodes.summary: The 2x2 Foster's Drill aims to improve offensive players' ability to read defenders and make tactical decisions while attacking at full speed. It requires proficiency in various dribbling and finishing moves. The drill involves two offensive and two defensive players, with the offense attacking the basket after receiving a pass and the defense sprinting to play. Key teaching points emphasize straight-line drives, attacking with speed, maintaining court spacing, controlled acceleration, and effective finishing. A common problem identified is a bad pass, with the solution being to eliminate the defender and focus on passer-receiver timing.

nodes.title: Drill: Celtic Fast Break Drill
nodes.summary: The provided text details various basketball drills and techniques focused on offensive skills, particularly lay-ups and ball handling under pressure. It covers the Celtic Fast Break Drill for finishing lay-ups from passes, the 1v0 Finishing Drill for transition lay-ups, and the Open Court Lay-ups Drill for developing offensive moves and finishes. Specific techniques like the stride stop are explained in detail. The text also addresses common problems such as mishandled passes and missed lay-ups, offering solutions and drills like the Baseline Shuffle Progression and Full Court 1v1 to improve ball handling against pressure and develop confidence. Teaching points are provided for each drill, emphasizing aspects like balance, footwork, ball protection, and attacking defenders.

nodes.title: Drill: 1v2
nodes.summary: The text describes the '1v2' basketball drill, focusing on an offensive player's ability to remain patient, protect the ball, and advance it up court against two defenders. It outlines the drill's objective, required pre-requisite skills, execution steps, and key teaching points for offensive players. The text also identifies a common problem of struggling in 1v1 open court situations and proposes simplifying drills with specific named drills (Foster's 1v1 Drill and Open Court Lay-up Drill) as a solution to improve offensive moves, finishes, and decision-making against live defense.

nodes.title: Drill: Foster's 1v1 Drill
nodes.summary:
## Drill: Foster's 1v1 Drill

|  Objective | To read a defender’s positioning in the open court and make the appropriate tactical decision while attacking full speed.  |
| --- | --- |
|  Pre-requisites | Speed dribble with both hands; hesitation move; in-n-out move; crossover move; lay-up; power lay-up and crossover lay-up.  |
|  Drill Execution | Offensive player starts on the baseline and the defender starts at the free throw line with a ball. Defender passes to the offensive player, sprints to half  |

nodes.title: 3v1 FAST BREAK
nodes.summary: The text describes the 3v1 Fast Break, emphasizing its strategic conversion into a 2v1 to exploit the lone defender. It outlines two main attack methods: the ball handler driving or passing to wings, and details how to create spacing and decision-making for offensive players. The document argues that a 3v1 can be less effective than a 2v1 due to spacing issues and provides questions to guide players' decision-making during such breaks. It also suggests using specific drills to practice and improve 3v1 fast break execution.

nodes.title: Drill: 3v3 Army Drill
nodes.summary: The text describes a 3v3 Army Drill focused on quick attacks, lay-up finishes under pressure, and decision-making. It outlines the objective, required pre-requisite skills (speed dribble, lay-ups, passes), the execution of the drill involving offensive and defensive players starting on the baseline and free throw line, and a progression where the drill becomes 3v1 if the ball goes to a wing player. Key teaching points emphasize spreading the floor, attacking together, creating 2v1 situations, and scoring quickly with limited passes.

nodes.title: 3v2 FAST BREAK
nodes.summary: The text provides a comprehensive overview of the 3v2 Fast Break in basketball, detailing its various scenarios, alignments, and strategic approaches. It contrasts middle breaks, which rely on a primary playmaker, with sideline breaks, which distribute playmaking responsibilities. The document outlines the advantages and disadvantages of each philosophy and presents a series of critical questions for coaches and players to consider when developing transition principles. These principles are presented as a flexible guide to enhance team coordination and performance during fast breaks, emphasizing that game situations ultimately dictate the best play.

nodes.title: Games
nodes.summary:
## Games

The games are similar to the 2v1 Games with an additional player. Once you have introduced all the different break scenarios, and want to use the games and drills to train the concepts, rather than introducing and teaching new skills, the drills and games provide an easy progression to move from 2v2 to 3v3 to 4v4 or 5v5 with the same basic rules. This adds efficiency to a practice setting as you review the rules one time for three or four drills, rather than teaching new rules every time you expand or change the drill.

nodes.title: Game: Rabbit
nodes.summary: This document describes a basketball drill called 'Rabbit'. The objective is to handle the ball in the open court, rebound aggressively, and make good decisions. Prerequisites include basic dribbling and passing skills. The drill involves two teams (A and B) with specific player roles and movements, creating live-play scenarios like 3v2 fast breaks and offensive rebounds. Key teaching points emphasize spacing, teamwork, quick scoring, and attacking open areas.

nodes.title: Drill: 3v2 Continuous Point
nodes.summary: This document describes the '3v2 Continuous Point' basketball drill, designed to enhance point guard decision-making and wing player lane-filling and finishing. It requires basic dribbling and passing skills. The drill involves a continuous full-court game where the offensive team stays on offense after scoring, and the defensive team rotates. A designated point guard remains on offense throughout. Key teaching points emphasize proactive play, attacking the basket, creating advantages, and forcing defensive reactions.

nodes.title: Game: 3v3 Hockey
nodes.summary: This document describes a 3v3 Hockey basketball drill focused on handling backcourt pressure, creating transition baskets, and finishing lay-ups. It outlines the objective, required pre-requisite skills (including various dribbling and lay-up techniques), and detailed drill execution. The drill involves teams rotating in and out of play after scoring or being scored upon, with specific rules for ball movement, defense, and out-of-bounds situations. Key teaching points emphasize court vision, using space dribbles, attacking the basket, and decision-making during offensive plays.

nodes.title: Game: 2v3/3v2
nodes.summary: This text describes a basketball drill called '2v3/3v2' with the objective of developing patience under pressure, ball protection, and advancing the ball. It lists necessary prerequisite skills and details the drill execution, which involves alternating between 2v3 and 3v2 offensive and defensive scenarios. Key teaching points focus on offensive movement, ball handling, attacking the basket, defensive strategies, and teamwork.

nodes.title: Practice
nodes.summary:
## Practice

When observing players play transition games, several mistakes occur frequently:

1. Too much dribbling
2. Pass too late – either the defense had recovered or the offensive player is flat-footed
3. Too congested – lack of spacing
4. Pass too early – (i.e. a post player not expecting the ball at the top of the key when he is sprinting to the rim)
5. Too slow developing
6. Pass to the wrong player – poor decision-making

nodes.title: Problem: Too much dribbling
nodes.summary:
## Problem: Too much dribbling

**Solution:** Limit the number of dribbles. Use any of the games, but limit players to two or three dribbles each. Or, play any of the games, but use 3-2-1 Rules: the first player has three dribbles to use; the second player has two dribbles; the third player has one dribble, and then the offense cannot dribble for the remainder of its possession. The objective is to get the ball moving.

nodes.title: Problem: Pass too late
nodes.summary:
## Problem: Pass too late

**Solution:** Encourage the early pass. Players often play the drill, not the game. They learn to jump stop at the free throw line (three-point line), and they follow directions regardless of the situation. Rather than pass to the player cutting to the rim, they take one extra dribble to jump stop at the top of the key. Work on passing off the dribble and finding the open teammate as soon as he is open.

nodes.title: Problem: Too congested
nodes.summary:
## Problem: Too congested

**Solution:** If the key becomes too congested, the ball handler likely waited too long to pass or one of the wings did not read the ball handler’s penetration and cut into his lane. Change the players’ thinking from attacking 3v2 to creating a 2v1. If the two defenders sit back and protect the basket, find the shooter and make the open three-point shot.

44

nodes.title: Problem: Pass too early
nodes.summary: The text addresses the problem of passing too early in basketball, which can lead to defensive advantages and failed plays. The solution emphasizes understanding teammates' strengths and weaknesses, forcing the defense to commit before passing, and being aggressive when appropriate. Player development is aided by experience and feedback, with a recommended teaching approach of using questions to foster understanding rather than direct criticism.

nodes.title: Problem: Too slow developing
nodes.summary:
## Problem: Too slow developing

Solution: Use the shot clock. Give players a limited amount of time to shoot (7-10 seconds). The goal is to play fast, but also under control and to get good shots. However, to score in transition, players must make decisions at a faster pace.

nodes.title: Problem: Pass to the wrong player
nodes.summary:
## Problem: Pass to the wrong player

Solution: Players need to know their teammates and read the defense. If players make the pass to the wrong player, they likely are not seeing the defender – they focus their attention on protecting the ball from their defender and making a move rather than seeing the whole court and finding the most open player. Develop players' confidence with the ball (Chapter 2) and use the games so players get more experience in transition situations.

nodes.title: 4v3 FAST BREAK
nodes.summary: The text outlines strategies for a four-man fast break, advocating for a two-wave attack rather than a single wave to avoid congesting the floor. It details the role of the trailer in the second wave and poses key questions for players to consider regarding lane filling, open spots, offensive advantages, and defensive alignment. The document strongly emphasizes the underutilization of communication in transition, providing specific examples of how posts can communicate their positions and intentions, and how verbal cues can inform the ball handler of available passing options, thereby enhancing court vision.

nodes.title: Games
nodes.summary: The text describes two basketball drills: '3v4/4v3' and '4v4 Transition'. Both drills focus on offensive and defensive strategies, ball protection, decision-making under pressure, and creating scoring opportunities. The '3v4/4v3' game emphasizes patience, ball protection, and exploiting transitions, with specific execution steps and teaching points on player movement and attacking defenders. The '4v4 Transition' game introduces width and depth in spacing, aggressive attacking to create 2v1 situations, and recovering into play after turnovers or missed shots to create fast breaks. Both drills list common pre-requisite skills and provide specific teaching points for effective execution.

nodes.title: Practice
nodes.summary:
## Practice

Many problems in a 4v3 or 5v4 break involve spacing, which is covered in more detail in the next chapter, or basic fundamental ideas and skills, which are covered in the 2v1 and 3v2 sections. The biggest difference is facing a diamond-type press with four defenders against three offensive players. Against back court pressure, players must be strong with the ball and exhibit patience. Pressure works when it forces the offense to make decisions and plays faster than the offense wants. By remaining patient, and relaxing under pressure, the offensive player can see the defense's vulnerabilities and attack accordingly.

If players struggle passing and receiving, review the games and drills in Chapter 3.

nodes.title: 5v4 BREAK
nodes.summary: The text details strategies for offensive breaks, particularly 5v4 situations, emphasizing the influence of coaching philosophy on break design and the importance of fundamental skills. It outlines various break structures, such as numbered and two-wave breaks, and provides a set of questions for players to consider during a break to identify and exploit defensive weaknesses. The document explains how to attack disorganized defenses by cutting to open spaces and making extra passes, and conversely, how defenses with a man advantage squeeze space to hinder the offense. It introduces Diamond Spacing as a principle to counter back court pressure and highlights the importance of patience and spacing. The text also describes specific drills, a 4v5/5v4 game and a 5v5 Transition game, to practice these concepts, detailing their objectives, prerequisites, execution, and key teaching points.

nodes.title: CONCLUSION
nodes.summary: The text discusses transition basketball, outlining constant concepts like spreading the floor, optimal 2v1 breaks, sprinting lanes, creating spacing, passing ahead, and making high-percentage plays. It then shifts to the importance of court spacing in offense, emphasizing teamwork, player anticipation, maintaining floor balance and spacing, adjusting positions as the ball moves, filling space, and using principles to drive motion offenses. Specific strategies like dividing the court into segments and using perimeter spots are also mentioned.

nodes.title: CUT & REPLACE
nodes.summary: The text describes the concept of 'cut and replace' in basketball, where offensive players without the ball read the game to get open, create opportunities for teammates, or move the defense. It highlights that cuts are not always for receiving a pass but can be to open lanes or create space. Examples include a post player creating a lane for a ball handler and a pick-and-roll scenario. The text also touches upon teaching methods like MacKay's segments, emphasizing player anticipation and the need for screeners to enter specific segments, while other players vacate them. Finally, it notes that both ball handlers and off-the-ball players must address certain questions.

nodes.title: Ball Handler
nodes.summary:
## Ball Handler

- Do I have a driving lane?
- Can I use the dribble to create a shot for a teammate?
Is a teammate open?
- Is a teammate in a more dangerous position (for instance, if I throw a skip pass to the opposite wing, will the low post have deep position in the paint)?
- Who has the best match-up? Who has the hot hand?

nodes.title: Off-the-Ball Players
nodes.summary:
## Off-the-Ball Players

- Am I in a dangerous position?

- Am I in a passing lane?
- Can I make a cut to clear the help defense and create a more dangerous position for a teammate?
- Can I cut to get open for a shot?
- Can I set a screen for a teammate?
- Can I clear the area for dribble penetration?
- Is the ball handler in trouble? Does he need someone to cut to relieve the ball pressure?

nodes.title: STRING SPACING
nodes.summary: The text explains the concept of 'string spacing' in basketball, emphasizing maintaining optimal distance between teammates to create offensive opportunities. It outlines three primary player movements (flare, cut backdoor, loop) when a teammate dribbles, and how these, combined with positional segments, help anticipate cuts. The importance of player movement and relocation to counter defensive help is highlighted, along with specific scenarios and decisions for both perimeter and post players. The text also provides a set of questions for the ball handler to consider and details two small-sided games, '4v4 Cut Throat' and '4v4 Canada Rules,' designed to teach and reinforce these spacing and movement principles through drills and modified gameplay.

nodes.title: Game: 4v4 Wildcat Rules
nodes.summary: The text describes the '4v4 Wildcat Rules' game, focusing on penetrating and finishing around the basket. It outlines the objective, necessary pre-requisite skills, and the execution of the drill, including how possession changes. Key teaching points emphasize offensive movement, spacing, and shooting readiness. Following the game, coaches are instructed to analyze player mistakes, identify the root cause (decision-making, movement, or technical skills), and then use specific drills like String Spacing Shooting, I-Shooting, and 2v2 Penetrate-and-Pitch to address these breakdowns before returning to game play.

nodes.title: Drill: String Spacing Shooting
nodes.summary: This text describes a basketball drill called 'String Spacing Shooting' designed to improve basic movement and spacing during dribble penetration. It outlines the drill's objective, necessary pre-requisite skills, and provides detailed execution steps for three variations: Flare, Follow, and Corner Outlet. Key teaching points focus on offensive strategy, player positioning, defensive reactions, and fundamental shooting techniques.

nodes.title: Drill: I-Shooting Drill
nodes.summary: The I-Shooting Drill is designed to practice basic post player movement in response to dribble penetration. It requires players to have mastered skills like speed dribbling and various passes. The drill involves two players, one starting on the wing (L1) and the other under the basket (L2). L1 attacks the paint and makes a pass to L2, then penetrates further while L2 moves to the short corner. L1 then passes to L2 for a shot, after which players switch roles. Key coaching points emphasize proper passing techniques, body positioning, and readiness to receive the ball and shoot or finish.

nodes.title: Game: 2v2 Penetrate and Pitch
nodes.summary: The text describes the '2v2 Penetrate and Pitch' game, focusing on dribble penetration and passing to create scoring opportunities. It outlines the objective, necessary skills (speed dribble, change of direction, spacing, catch-and-shoot, push pass), the drill execution involving offensive and defensive players on a half court, and a progression limiting passes. Key teaching points emphasize attacking the basket, making simple plays, and forcing defensive reactions.

nodes.title: POST SPACING
nodes.summary: The text discusses post spacing as a crucial offensive concept, emphasizing the need for movement away from the ball when it enters the low post to prevent traps and double-teams. It outlines three primary options for the passer on a post entry: relocating, executing a give-and-go, or screening away. Each option involves specific player movements and spacing adjustments to create scoring opportunities. The text also details how multiple offensive players on the strong side can cut and how spacing can exploit defensive rotations, leading to open shots, particularly when the defense attempts to double-team the post.

nodes.title: Games
nodes.summary:
## Games

Use 4v4 Cut Throat or 4v5 Games to practice ball and player movement when the defense traps on the low block. In Cut Throat, rather than play with a four-out alignment, use a three-out, one-in alignment; and reward the offense for getting the ball into the post; for instance, give one point for each post entry pass into the low block in addition to counting baskets or count any basket as two points if the offense scores off a cut related to low post play.

To play against a trap, force the defense to double team anytime the defense receives the ball on the low block. In 4v5, use the extra defender to trap on the low block. Also, to practice the full rotations, play 5v6 with the 6th man only there to trap on the low block.

nodes.title: Practice
nodes.summary:
## Practice

After watching the players play, decide the cause of the mistakes:

1. Do the players forget where to cut?
2. Do they cut too close to the post player?
3. Is the post player in a hurry to make a move?
4. Does the post player struggle to make the pass out of the double team? Is the pass deflected by the trappers or does a help defender steal the pass?

If the problem is the general movement, use the basic spacing concepts to create shooting drills. If the problem is the passing under pressure, use the Chapter 3 drills to practice passing and receiving skills.

The document outlines different types of cuts (across the face, backdoor, V-cut) and the four essential components for success: court spacing, reading the defense, squaring quickly, and accurate passing. It provides specific guidance for both the cutter and the passer, including decision-making questions and appropriate passing techniques based on defensive reactions. The text also introduces a practice game, '4v4 Cut Throat', with its objectives, rules, progressions, and teaching points to enhance these skills.

nodes.title: DRIBBLE-AT
nodes.summary: The text describes the 'dribble-at' basketball play, which offers two options: a backdoor cut or a dribble hand-off. The play is initiated by the ball handler dribbling at a teammate's defender. If the defender drops, a hand-off occurs; if the defender plays between the players, a backdoor cut is made. The text details the execution of both the hand-off (including a jump stop and screen) and the backdoor cut (a bounce pass leading to the basket). It also explains the dribble hand-off as a guard-to-guard or post-to-guard exchange, outlining the subsequent offensive actions for each scenario: flaring for a jump shot in guard-to-guard exchanges, and rolling to the basket in post-to-guard exchanges to exploit defensive switches or hedges.

nodes.title: Games
nodes.summary:
## Games

Use different 3v3 and 4v4 games like 4v4 Princeton Rules and 3v3 Weave to develop the dribble-at skill.

### Questions to Resolve

1. How is my defender defending me? Can I penetrate to draw help (or score) or am I penetrating at my teammate's defender for the hand-off?
2. How is my teammate's defender playing him?
3. Which way is the defender leaning?
4. Where is his weight?
5. Where are his eyes?
6. Is the post open for a backdoor cut?

## (2) The Side Pick-and-Roll

Take the defender below the level of the screen, so the screener gets the right angle (Figure 13). If the defense hedges hard or traps, pass to the middle and then the screener. Attack aggressively, but show patience against a switch (Figure 14).

nodes.title: Using an On-Ball Screen
nodes.summary:
## Using an On-Ball Screen

Attack the on-ball screen to turn the corner and get to the basket. However, the defense dictates the right play. If the ball handler's defender gets caught on the screen or goes over top, turn the corner and force the screener's defender to stop you. If you cannot beat the hedging defender immediately, use a fan dribble to create space. A fan dribble is a lateral shuffle dribble with shoulders squared to the basket. If the screener's defender offers no resistance, attack the rim.

nodes.title: Defense Goes Under - No Hedge
nodes.summary:
## Defense Goes Under - No Hedge

If the ball handler's defender goes under the screen, and the screener's defender does not hedge, square your shoulders and attack down hill. Do not let the defense off the hook; attack your defender and make him stop the ball.

nodes.title: Defense Hedges
nodes.summary:
## Defense Hedges

If the screener's defender hedges use at least two dribbles to extend the hedge (Figure 15). The cardinal sin of pick-and-roll basketball is to pick up the dribble. If the hedge is flat (defender keeps his back to the baseline) or soft (steps out with a hand and a foot, not his whole body), stay low and attack the hedge, using the two dribbles to turn the corner. Best case, you beat the hedge and turn the corner; worst case, the hedger prevents you from turning the corner, but you extend the hedge and force the defense to switch. If you pick up your dribble when you see the flat hedge or soft show, you bail out the defense, as your defender recovers easily and there is no separation between the screener and his defender.

nodes.title: Defense Traps
nodes.summary: This text describes offensive strategies for players facing defensive hedges or traps. The text emphasizes avoiding turning your back or picking up the dribble when trapped. It also explains how to exploit the space created by aggressive traps by passing out or attacking lanes, and how beating one defender creates an offensive advantage.

nodes.title: Slip the Screen
nodes.summary:
## Slip the Screen

If the defense shows the hedge or trap too early, the screener can slip the screen (Figure 21). As he runs to set the screen, if he feels his defender move out of position and give away the lane to the basket, he cuts to the basket rather than setting the screen.

nodes.title: SETTING A SCREEN
nodes.summary:
## SETTING A SCREEN

Setting a screen seems like a simple skill, yet many teams set ineffective and illegal screens. To set a good screen, the screener:

- Headhunts: the screener must find the defender and move to him rather than relying on the offensive player to run the defender into the screen.
- Jump stops a half step before running into the defender.
- Sets a strong screen with a wide base.
- Communicates verbally ("Use me!) or non-verbally (closed fist) with his teammate so the teammate knows that he is setting a screen for him.
- Moves opposite the cutter – if the cutter cuts to the basket, the screener rolls high; if the cutter cuts high, the screener rolls to the basket.

It also advises passers to have broad awareness and pass away from the defense, suggesting communication during learning and encouraging anticipation for automatic reactions.
